tier_reason: bench/README.md tables match every number in the record. The harness is public (bench/bench_test.go): it runs wasman, wazero v1.12.0 (interpreter and compiler configs), wagon v0.4.0 and life through their public APIs, and checks the expected result on every iteration. The page states Go 1.24, the exact command `go test -bench . -benchmem ./bench` (default flags) and the CPU (Apple M3), which is everything tier A asks for.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.24 (per bench/README.md); go test -bench . -benchmem ./bench with default Go flags; fixtures compiled from .wat with wat2wasm and checked in. bench/go.mod at HEAD declares go 1.25.0 and pins wazero v1.12.0, wagon v0.4.0 (via replace) and life at a 2019 commit. Every timed iteration checks the returned value against a constant.
corrections.caveats: Self-benchmarked by the author. Each row is a single run with no variance reported, and run-to-run noise is visible: the wasman interpreter's Fib reads 974,787 ns in the main table and 1,120,975 ns in the JIT table, 15% apart, which is larger than the 1.08x MemRW margin over wazero's interpreter. Workloads are very small (Fib(20) is about 13.5k calls). The Instantiate sub-benchmark for wazero creates and closes a whole wazero Runtime on every iteration (NewRuntimeWithConfig + Instantiate + Close, with no CompiledModule reuse), so the 6.6x instantiation win over wazero includes runtime setup and teardown that wasman's row does not pay. The README bolds wasman-jit on Sum even though its 27,112 ns is 1% slower than wazero-compiler's 26,850 ns. The EPYC 7K62 claims (Sum 2.0x, MemRW 1.6x ahead, Fib 1.6x behind) are ratios only, with no table. Only Go engines are compared: cgo runtimes (wasmtime-go, wasmer-go) are excluded, so there is no comparison with wasmtime, wasmer, V8 or WAMR. The JIT result is mixed: ahead of wazero's compiler on memory-bound code (MemRW 1.8x, Sort 1.3x), level on Sum and Dispatch, and behind on Fib (9%), Hash (9%), Mandel (3%) and Indirect (1.4x). LICENSE carries 'Copyright (c) 2020 @mathetake', the author of gasm, which became wazero, so wasman shares ancestry with its main baseline. Interpreter and JIT correctness fixes landed 2026-08-16 to 08-19, after the documented numbers (host-call resolution, toll return sentinel). None of them touches the benchmark workloads, which have no imports and no TollStation. Wazero is the Go incumbent but not one of the listed baselines.

notes: The record is accurate; the README's ratios (1.1-1.8x vs wazero-interp, 1.5-2.4x vs wagon, about 2x vs life, 3-14x instantiate) all check out against the table values. Shortcomings to record: single runs with noise comparable to the smallest win, a wazero Instantiate row that rebuilds a Runtime per iteration, a mixed JIT result, a Go-only field, and an off-list baseline (wazero).

corrections.caveats: benchmark.md calls the numbers 'user-supplied measurements' and a 'preliminary snapshot'. There is one machine (Windows 11), and the runtime versions, runtime compiler flags, KinoRuntime preset/PGO settings, measurement date, workload hashes and per-run spread are all unrecorded. CoreMark is not bundled, and iwasm ran 30,000 iterations while the other two ran 60,000. The final CRC differs between iwasm (0x5275) and wasm3/KinoRuntime (0xbd59). That is consistent with the different iteration counts, since CoreMark's final CRC accumulates over iterations, and all three logs report validation passed. Fibonacci timing uses the in-guest clock through each runtime's WASI clock, and the repeat count is unrecorded. The baselines were Windows builds of unknown configuration. WAMR's core/config.h enables labels-as-values (computed-goto) dispatch only under __GNUC__, so an MSVC or clang-cl build of iwasm falls back to switch dispatch, which may explain much of the 2.5x gap to iwasm. wasm3 on Windows may be similarly disadvantaged. The repo carries CoreMark-trained PGO presets, which is a tuning risk if one built the measured binary. The project is very new (first commit 2026-09-30, 6 commits, single author), and correctness fixes landed 2026-10-08/09 (live register tracking below wide-arithmetic operands; integer overflow in buffer-read bounds checks), possibly after the undated measurements.

notes: The record is accurate and the numbers match docs/benchmark.md; tier C stands, since these are first-party, user-supplied numbers with unrecorded runtime builds. Shortcomings to record: not reproducible (no runtime versions or flags, CoreMark not bundled, a single Windows machine), a possibly handicapped iwasm baseline (no computed-goto dispatch on non-GNU Windows builds), CoreMark-trained PGO presets, 0 stars, and unverifiable console production claims.
